intro: You have a name. You have a birthday. You like some things and not others. You can do some things and are still learning others. All of that is you. No one else is just like you.
You live with people who take care of you. That is your family. Families come in many shapes. Some are big. Some are small. In every one, people help each other and tell stories.

You also go to school. There you meet kids who are like you and not like you. There are rules there. There are rules at home too. This unit is about who you are, who you live with and why rules help us live together.
bigQuestion: Who am I, who are my people, and how do rules help us live together?

timeline.t: Mom says your name. It is your name and no one else's.
You wash your hands first. That is a rule at home. It keeps germs away.
Your brother zips your coat. Family members help each other.
The crossing guard holds up her sign. The cars stop. You cross.
You sit down. The bus stops fast. Sitting keeps you safe.
The class picks three rules. Be safe. Be kind. Listen. You vote.
One swing, five kids. Count to twenty. Everyone gets a turn.
You draw a poster about you. Things you like. Things you can do.
Paint spills. You say sorry and help clean up. You made it right.
Shoes off at the door. Grandma's rule. She does not like mud.
Grandpa tells his story about the two-dollar boots. Again.
Your family sings the same song every night. That is a tradition.

words.d: the day of the year you were born
the people who love you and take care of you
a thing a family does again and again, year after year
the time before now, like long ago
not the same
a thing that tells you what to do or not do
the same chance for everyone
a person who guides a group and helps it

test.why: A birthday is the day of the year you were born.

test.q: Leo lives with just his mom. Is that a family?
choices: Only if he has a pet
test.why: A family can be big or small. What makes it a family is the care.

test.q: Ana's family eats together every Sunday. What is that?
test.why: A tradition is a thing a family does again and again.

test.q: How do we know about Grandpa's two-dollar boots?
choices: Grandpa and Great-Grandma tell the story
test.why: People who were there tell us. Their stories are clues about the past.

test.q: Ana likes cats. Leo likes trucks. What does that show?
choices: They cannot be in the same class
They are different, and that is fine
test.why: Classmates are different in some ways. They can teach each other new things.

test.q: Why is there a rule about walking at the pool?
test.why: Wet ground is slippery. Running can make you fall.

test.q: Count to twenty, then give the next kid the swing. What does that rule do?
test.why: Everyone gets a turn. That is fair.

test.q: How did Room Twelve choose its rules?
test.why: The kids shared ideas and voted with dots. The top three rules won.

test.q: Sam spilled paint. What should he do to make it right?
choices: Say sorry and help clean up
test.why: To make it right means to fix what you did. Say sorry and help.

test.q: Who is a leader who stops cars so kids can cross?
test.why: The crossing guard holds up her sign and stops the cars. She keeps kids safe.

write.prompt: Pick one rule from your class or your home. Say what the rule is. Tell who could get hurt or feel sad without it. Tell why the rule is a good rule.
tips: Claim: name the rule and say it is a good rule.
Evidence: tell what happened in the reading when a rule was broken, like Sam falling or Leo grabbing the crayon.
Reasoning: say if your rule is about being safe, being fair or getting along.
The other side: say why someone might not like the rule, and why it still helps.

title: Me, My Family, My School

chapters.title: Who I Am and Who I Live With
chapters.bigQuestion: What makes me who I am, and who are the people I live with?

story.title: Grandpa Tells It Again
story.kicker: Four generations sit at one table. Grandpa has a story. Everyone has heard it before.
paragraphs: It is Sunday in Chicago. Ana's family sits down to eat. There is a lot of them. Ana. Her big brother Mateo. Her mom and dad. Her grandma and grandpa. And Great-Grandma Rosa, who is ninety years old. Seven people. One long table.
Ana passes the rice. Mateo pours the water. Grandma cuts the bread. Dad holds Great-Grandma's arm when she sits down. Everyone has a job. Everyone helps.

Then Grandpa clears his throat. Mateo grins. He knows what is coming. "When I was six," Grandpa says, "I walked to school in the snow. I had one pair of boots. They were my brother's old boots." Ana has heard this story ten times. She still likes it.
Great-Grandma Rosa laughs. "I bought those boots," she says. "They cost two dollars." The whole table laughs. Ana looks around. This is her family. These are her people.
story.think: Who sits at your table? What story does your family tell again and again?

lessons.title: My Name and My Birthday
lessons.mainIdea: Every person has a name and a birthday. They are part of who you are.
reading: Ana has a *name*. Her name is Ana Cruz. Someone picked that name for her. Her mom picked it. Ana was named for her great-grandma. Your name is yours. It tells people who you are.
Ana also has a *birthday*. A birthday is the day you were born. Ana was born on March third. Every year on March third, she turns one year older. This year she turned six.
Everyone in Ana's class has a name. Everyone has a birthday. No two people have the very same name and birthday. That makes each person special.

words.d: the word people call you by
the day of the year you were born

look.title: The Birthday Chart
look.text: Look at the chart on the wall. It has twelve boxes. One box for each month. Ana's name is in the March box. Leo's name is in the March box too. The July box is empty. No one in the class has a July birthday.
look.prompt: Which month has two names in it? What do Ana and Leo share?

check.q: What is a birthday?
choices: A day you get a new name
check.why: A birthday is the day of the year you were born. You have one every year.

check.q: Who picked Ana's name?
check.why: The reading says Ana's mom picked her name. Ana was named for her great-grandma.

check.q: What happens on your birthday each year?
check.why: Every year on March third, Ana turns one year older. Your birthday works the same way.

lessons.title: Things I Like and Can Do
lessons.mainIdea: What you like and what you can do are part of who you are.
reading: Ana likes to draw. She draws cats. She draws her house. Ana does not like loud noise. She covers her ears at parades. What you *like* is part of you.
Ana can tie her shoes. She learned last year. It was hard at first. Now it is easy. Ana cannot ride a bike yet. She is still learning. What you *can do* is part of you too.
Think about yourself. What do you like? What can you do? Maybe you can count to one hundred. Maybe you can swim. Each thing you learn makes you more you.

words.d: to enjoy a thing or want to do it
a thing you know how to do

look.title: Ana's Poster
look.text: Ana made a poster about herself. At the top it says ANA. There is a drawing of a cat. There is a drawing of a shoe with a bow. There is a drawing of a bike with a big X on it. Under the bike it says NOT YET.
look.prompt: What does each drawing tell you about Ana? What would you put on your poster?

check.q: What does Ana like to do?
check.why: The reading says Ana likes to draw. She draws cats and her house.

check.q: What can Ana do now that was hard before?
check.why: Ana learned to tie her shoes last year. It was hard at first. Now it is easy.

check.q: Ana cannot ride a bike. What does the reading say about that?
check.why: Ana cannot ride a bike yet. She is still learning. People learn new things all the time.

lessons.title: Families Come in Many Shapes
lessons.mainIdea: A family is the people who love you and take care of you. Families are not all the same size.
reading: A *family* is the people who take care of you. Ana lives with seven people. That is a big family. Her friend Leo lives with his mom. That is two people. Both are families.

Some kids live with a mom and a dad. Some live with one parent. Some live with a grandma. Some live with two moms or two dads. Some kids have a step-parent. Some are adopted. All of these are families.
A family can be big or small. It can live in one home or two homes. What makes a family is not the size. It is the care. Family members love each other and help each other.

words.d: the people who love you and take care of you

look.title: How Many People Live at Home?
look.prompt: Whose family is the biggest? Whose is the smallest? Are they all families?

check.q: What is a family?
choices: The people who take care of you
Only a mom, a dad and two kids
check.why: A family is the people who love you and take care of you. It can be many shapes.

check.q: Leo lives with his mom. Is that a family?
choices: Yes, two people can be a family
Only if a dad lives there too
check.why: A family can be big or small. Leo and his mom are a family.

check.q: What makes a family a family?
choices: The care people give each other
check.why: What makes a family is not the size. It is the care. Family members help each other.

lessons.title: We Help Each Other
lessons.mainIdea: People in a family have jobs, and they help each other.
reading: At dinner, Ana's family works as a team. Mateo pours water. Grandma cuts bread. Dad helps Great-Grandma sit down. Ana passes the rice. Each person does a *job*.
Kids can help too. Ana feeds the cat. She puts her toys away. Mateo takes out the trash. These jobs are small. But they matter. The home runs better when everyone helps.
Grown-ups help kids. They cook. They read stories. They take you to the doctor. Kids help grown-ups too. When a family helps each other, everyone feels safe.

words.d: a task you do to help

look.title: The Morning Rush
look.text: It is seven o'clock. Mom packs two lunches. Dad finds Ana's shoes. Mateo zips Ana's coat. Ana holds the door for Grandma. Grandma hands Mateo his hat. In five minutes, everyone is out the door.
look.prompt: Count the ways people helped. Who helped Ana? Who did Ana help?

check.q: What is Ana's job at home?
check.why: The reading says Ana feeds the cat and puts her toys away.

check.q: Why do small jobs matter?
choices: The home runs better when everyone helps
check.why: Small jobs matter. The home runs better when everyone helps.

check.q: Who helps whom in a family?
choices: Grown-ups and kids help each other
check.why: Grown-ups help kids. Kids help grown-ups too. Everyone helps each other.

lessons.title: Things We Do Every Year
lessons.mainIdea: A tradition is something a family does again and again.
reading: Every Sunday, Ana's family eats together. Every March, they make a cake for Ana. Every winter, they hang lights. These are *traditions*. A tradition is a thing you do again and again.
Families have different traditions. Leo and his mom make pancakes on Saturdays. Mia's family lights candles on special nights. Sam's family goes to the lake every summer.
Some traditions are big. A holiday is a big one. Some are small. A song at bedtime is a small one. Big or small, traditions bring a family together.

words.d: a thing a family does again and again, year after year
a special day people celebrate

look.title: The Same Cake
look.text: Look at the photo. It is Ana's birthday last year. There is a cake with pink frosting. Now look at this photo. It is Ana's birthday this year. Same pink cake. Grandma makes it every March. She learned it from Great-Grandma Rosa.
look.prompt: Why is the cake the same both years? What does your family do every year?

check.q: What is a tradition?
choices: A thing a family does again and again
A thing you do only once
check.why: A tradition is a thing a family does again and again, like Sunday dinner.

check.q: What is Leo's family tradition?
check.why: The reading says Leo and his mom make pancakes on Saturdays.

check.q: Do all families have the same traditions?
choices: Yes, every family does the same things
check.why: Families have different traditions. Leo makes pancakes. Mia lights candles. Sam goes to the lake.

lessons.title: Grandpa's Story From Long Ago
lessons.mainIdea: Family stories tell us what life was like long ago.
reading: Grandpa was a boy a long time ago. His family had one phone. It hung on the kitchen wall. It had a cord. There was no phone in his pocket. There was no computer at all.
Grandpa walked to school. He walked in the rain. He walked in the snow. He wore his brother's old boots. Great-Grandma Rosa bought those boots. They cost two dollars.
How do we know? Grandpa tells us. Great-Grandma was there too. A story from a person who was there is a clue about the *past*. The past is the time before now.

words.d: the time before now, like long ago

look.title: Then and Now
look.text: Look at the old photo. Grandpa is six. He stands in the snow. His coat is too big. His boots are too big. Now look at Ana's photo. She is six. She stands in the snow. Her coat fits. Her boots are new and pink.
look.prompt: What is the same in the two photos? What is different?

check.q: Where was Grandpa's phone when he was a boy?
check.why: Grandpa's family had one phone. It hung on the kitchen wall.

check.q: How did Grandpa get to school?
check.why: The reading says Grandpa walked to school, even in the rain and snow.

check.q: How do we know about Grandpa's boots?
choices: We read it in a book
check.why: Grandpa tells the story. Great-Grandma was there. People who were there give us clues about the past.

lessons.title: Same and Different
lessons.mainIdea: Classmates are the same in some ways and different in others, and that is good.
reading: Ana and Leo are in the same class. They both like to draw. They both have March birthdays. In those ways, they are the *same*.
Ana has a big family. Leo has a small one. Ana speaks Spanish at home. Leo speaks English. Ana likes cats. Leo likes trucks. In those ways, they are *different*.
Different is good. Leo teaches Ana about trucks. Ana teaches Leo a Spanish word. A class with many kinds of kids can learn many things.

words.d: just like another
not the same

look.title: Two Circles
look.text: The teacher draws two big circles. They overlap in the middle. One circle says ANA. One says LEO. In the middle she writes: likes to draw, March birthday. On Ana's side: big family, cats. On Leo's side: small family, trucks.
look.prompt: What goes in the middle? What would be in the middle for you and a friend?

check.q: How are Ana and Leo the same?
check.why: The reading says they both like to draw and both have March birthdays.

check.q: How are Ana and Leo different?
choices: Ana likes cats and Leo likes trucks
check.why: Ana likes cats. Leo likes trucks. That is one way they are different.

check.q: Why is it good that classmates are different?
choices: So they never have to talk
They can teach each other new things
check.why: Leo teaches Ana about trucks. Ana teaches Leo a word. Different kids can learn from each other.

lessons.title: My Class Is a Group
lessons.mainIdea: Your class is a group of many different people who belong together.
reading: Ana's class has twenty kids. Some are tall. Some are short. Some have big families. Some have small ones. They come from many places. They are one class.
A *group* is people who are together. A family is a group. A class is a group. In a group, each person matters. Each one adds something.
Ana adds her drawings. Leo adds his jokes. Mia adds her singing. Sam adds his help. Take one away, and the class is not the same.

words.d: people who are together and belong together

look.title: The Class Photo
look.text: Look at the class photo. Twenty kids stand in three rows. Ana is in front. She is short. Sam is in back. He is tall. Some kids smile. One kid makes a silly face. Every face is different. Every kid is in the same photo.
look.prompt: Find one thing that is different about each kid. What do they all share?

check.q: What is a group?
check.why: A group is people who are together and belong together, like a class.

check.q: Which of these is a group?
check.why: A family is a group. So is a class. A group has more than one person.

check.q: What does Mia add to the class?
check.why: The reading says Mia adds her singing. Ana adds drawings. Leo adds jokes.

choices: A day you help at home
review.why: A birthday is the day of the year you were born.

review.q: Leo lives with just his mom. What is that?
review.why: A family can be big or small. What makes it a family is the care.

review.q: Ana feeds the cat every day. What is that?
choices: A job that helps her family
review.why: Feeding the cat is Ana's job. Small jobs help the whole family.

review.q: Ana's family eats together every Sunday. What is that called?
review.why: A tradition is a thing a family does again and again.

review.q: How do we know what Grandpa's childhood was like?
review.why: Grandpa was there. His story is a clue about the past.

review.q: Ana likes cats. Leo likes trucks. What does that show?
choices: They are different, and that is fine
review.why: Classmates are different in some ways. Different kids can teach each other new things.

chapters.title: Rules at School and at Home
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do we have rules, and who gets to make them?

story.title: Three Rules for Room Twelve
story.kicker: It is the first day of school. The class has no rules yet. So they make their own.
paragraphs: It is the first day of school. Twenty kids sit on the rug in Room Twelve. Ms. Park sits in a small chair. "This is our room," she says. "We need some rules. But I will not make them. You will."

The kids talk. Leo says, "No hitting." Mia says, "Be quiet when someone is talking." Sam says, "No running in the hall. I fell last year." Ana says, "Say sorry if you are mean." Ms. Park writes every idea on the board. There are twelve ideas.

"Twelve is too many," Ms. Park says. "Let's pick three." The kids look at the list. Some ideas are almost the same. They put those together. Then each kid gets three sticky dots. They stick a dot next to the rules they like best.
The three rules with the most dots win. Be safe. Be kind. Listen. Ms. Park writes them big on a chart. Every kid signs the chart. Now the rules belong to them.
story.think: Why did Ms. Park let the kids make the rules instead of making them herself?

lessons.title: Rules Keep Us Safe
lessons.mainIdea: Many rules keep people from getting hurt.
reading: Sam fell in the hall last year. He was running. He hit his head. It hurt. Now Sam knows why there is a *rule*. A rule tells you what to do or not do. No running in the hall.
Many rules keep us *safe*. Walk, do not run. Keep your hands to yourself. Look both ways before you cross. Sit down on the bus. Each rule stops someone from getting hurt.
Think of a rule at your school. Ask yourself: who could get hurt without it? If you can name someone, that rule is a safety rule.

words.d: a thing that tells you what to do or not do
not hurt and not in danger

look.title: The Wet Floor
look.text: Look at the hall. The floor is wet. There is a yellow sign. It says WET FLOOR. Leo walks slowly. His shoes stay under him. Behind him, a big kid runs. His feet slide. Down he goes.
look.prompt: Who followed the rule? Who did not? What happened to each one?

check.q: What is a rule?
choices: A thing that tells you what to do or not do
check.why: A rule tells you what to do or not do, like walk in the hall.

check.q: Why is there a rule about running in the hall?
choices: Someone could fall and get hurt
check.why: Sam ran and fell and hit his head. The rule keeps kids from getting hurt.

check.q: Which rule keeps you safe?
choices: Look both ways before you cross
check.why: Looking both ways keeps you from getting hit by a car. That is a safety rule.

lessons.title: Rules Are Fair
lessons.mainIdea: Rules make things fair so everyone gets a turn.
reading: There is one swing. Five kids want it. Without a rule, the biggest kid gets it every time. That is not *fair*. Fair means everyone gets the same chance.
So there is a rule. Count to twenty. Then give the next kid a turn. Now all five kids swing. The rule made it fair.
Rules help people get along too. Raise your hand to talk. Then everyone gets heard. Clean up your own mess. Then no one does all the work. Fair rules stop fights before they start.

words.d: the same chance for everyone

look.title: The Cookie Plate
look.text: Look at the plate. There are ten cookies. There are five kids. Mia says, "Two each." Everyone takes two. The plate is empty. No one cries. Now imagine there was no rule. Sam grabs six. Ana gets none.
look.prompt: Which way is fair? How do you know?

check.q: What does fair mean?
check.why: Fair means everyone gets the same chance, like every kid getting a turn on the swing.

check.q: What does the swing rule do?
choices: Lets the biggest kid swing longest
check.why: Count to twenty, then give the next kid a turn. All five kids get to swing.

check.q: Why do we raise our hands to talk?
check.why: If everyone talks at once, no one is heard. Raising hands makes it fair.

lessons.title: Rules at Home
lessons.mainIdea: Homes have rules too, and grown-ups make most of them.
reading: Ana's family has rules at *home*. Wash your hands before you eat. Shoes off at the door. Lights out at eight. Grandma made the shoes rule. She does not like mud on her floor.
Every home has its own rules. Leo's rule is no TV before homework. Mia's rule is feed the fish first. Rules at home can be different from house to house.
Home rules have reasons. Clean hands keep germs away. Lights out means good sleep. Ask a grown-up why a rule is there. There is almost always a reason.

words.d: the place where you live

look.title: The Sign on the Fridge
look.text: Look at Ana's fridge. There is a paper on it. It says: Hands washed. Shoes off. Toys away. Lights out at eight. Next to each rule there is a small drawing. Great-Grandma Rosa drew them. She cannot read English, but she can read the pictures.
look.prompt: Why did Great-Grandma draw pictures? Which rule is a safety rule?

check.q: Who made the shoes rule at Ana's house?
check.why: Grandma made the shoes rule. She does not like mud on her floor.

check.q: Are home rules the same in every house?
choices: Yes, every house is the same
No, each home has its own rules
check.why: Leo's rule is no TV before homework. Mia's rule is feed the fish first. Homes differ.

check.q: Why does Ana wash her hands before she eats?
check.why: Clean hands keep germs away. That is the reason for the rule.

lessons.title: On the Bus and at the Pool
lessons.mainIdea: Different places have different rules because they have different dangers.
reading: On the bus, the rule is sit down. Stay in your seat. The bus stops fast. A kid who is standing can fall. The bus driver makes the rules on the bus.
At the pool, the rule is walk, do not run. The ground is wet. Wet ground is slippery. The lifeguard makes the rules at the pool. If she blows a whistle, you stop and listen.
Every *place* has its own rules. The rules fit the place. A pool rule is about water. A bus rule is about riding. Look at a place. You can guess its rules.

words.d: a spot where things happen, like a pool or a bus

look.title: How Many Rules Are Posted?
look.cite: signs Ana counted on a walk
look.prompt: Which place has the most rules? Why might a pool need more rules than a library?

check.q: Why do you sit down on the bus?
choices: The bus stops fast and you could fall
check.why: The bus stops fast. A kid who is standing can fall. Sitting keeps you safe.

check.q: Who makes the rules at the pool?
check.why: The lifeguard makes the rules at the pool. When she blows the whistle, you listen.

check.q: Why is there a walking rule at the pool?
choices: Running is too fast for fun
check.why: The ground is wet. Wet ground is slippery. Running can make you fall.

lessons.title: Our Class Makes Rules
lessons.mainIdea: A class can make its own rules by sharing ideas and voting.
reading: Ms. Park did not make the rules for Room Twelve. The kids did. First, everyone shared an idea. Then they put the same ideas together. Then they voted.
A *vote* is when each person picks what they want. Each kid got three dots. They put the dots by the rules they liked. The three rules with the most dots won.
Be safe. Be kind. Listen. The kids picked those. So the kids follow them. When you help make a rule, you want to keep it.

words.d: to pick what you want so a group can decide

look.title: The Dot Vote
look.prompt: Which three rules won? Why did no gum lose?

check.q: Who made the rules for Room Twelve?
check.why: Ms. Park let the kids share ideas and vote. The kids made the rules.

check.q: What is a vote?
choices: When each person picks what they want
check.why: A vote is when each person picks what they want. The group counts the picks.

check.q: Why do the kids want to keep their rules?
check.why: When you help make a rule, you want to keep it. The rules belong to the kids.

lessons.title: When a Rule Is Broken
lessons.mainIdea: When you break a rule, you can make it right.
reading: Leo grabbed a crayon from Mia. Mia cried. Leo broke a rule. Be kind. Ms. Park did not yell. She asked, "What happened? How can you make it right?"
Leo gave the crayon back. He said, "I am sorry." He asked, "Can I use it when you are done?" Mia said yes. Leo made it *right*. To make it right means to fix what you did.
Everyone breaks a rule sometimes. What matters is what you do next. Tell the truth. Say sorry. Fix it if you can. Then try again.

words.d: to fix a wrong you did

look.title: The Spilled Paint
look.text: Sam runs to the sink. He bumps the table. Blue paint spills on Ana's picture. Ana's face falls. Sam stops. He looks at the paint. He looks at Ana. He gets paper towels. He says, "I am sorry. I ran. Can I help you make a new one?"
look.prompt: What rule did Sam break? What three things did he do to make it right?

check.q: What rule did Leo break?
check.why: Leo grabbed a crayon and made Mia cry. That broke the rule be kind.

check.q: What does it mean to make it right?
check.why: To make it right means to fix the wrong. Leo gave the crayon back and said sorry.

check.q: What did Ms. Park do when Leo broke the rule?
choices: She asked how he could make it right
check.why: Ms. Park did not yell. She asked what happened and how Leo could make it right.

lessons.title: Turns, Ears and the Truth
lessons.mainIdea: A good classmate takes turns, listens and tells the truth.
reading: There is one red marker. Ana uses it. Then she hands it to Leo. Then Leo hands it to Mia. That is *taking turns*. Everyone gets a chance.
Mia is telling a story. Sam looks at her. He does not talk. He waits. That is *listening*. It shows Mia that she matters.
Ana broke a cup. No one saw. Ana tells Ms. Park anyway. That is telling the truth. It is hard sometimes. But people trust you when you tell the truth.

words.d: one person goes, then the next
looking at the speaker and hearing the words
what really happened

look.title: Circle Time
look.text: Twenty kids sit in a circle. There is one talking stick. Only the kid with the stick can talk. Leo has it. He tells about his dog. Every eye is on Leo. When he is done, he passes the stick to Ana. Now every eye is on Ana.
look.prompt: How does the talking stick help kids take turns? How does it help them listen?

check.q: Ana uses the marker, then hands it to Leo. What is that?
check.why: One person goes, then the next. That is taking turns.

check.q: How does Sam show he is listening?
choices: He looks at Mia and waits
check.why: Sam looks at Mia. He does not talk. He waits. That is listening.

check.q: Why should you tell the truth even when it is hard?
check.why: People trust you when you tell the truth. Ana told about the cup even though no one saw.

lessons.title: Leaders Who Help
lessons.mainIdea: A teacher, a principal and a crossing guard are leaders who help keep school working.
reading: Ms. Park is a teacher. She helps the class learn. She helps kids follow the rules. A teacher is a *leader*. A leader is a person who guides a group.
Mr. Green is the *principal*. He leads the whole school. He makes rules for every class. He walks the halls. If a kid is hurt or lost, he helps.
Ms. Lee is the crossing guard. She stands at the corner. She holds a red sign. She stops the cars. Then kids can cross. She is a leader too. Leaders help people stay safe.

words.d: a person who guides a group and helps it
the leader of the whole school

look.title: The Corner at Eight
look.text: Look at the corner by the school. Cars go by fast. Ms. Lee steps into the street. She holds up her red sign. Every car stops. Ana, Leo and ten more kids walk across. Ms. Lee waves. Then she steps back. The cars go again.
look.prompt: What would happen at the corner without Ms. Lee? How is she a leader?

check.q: What is a leader?
choices: A person who guides a group
check.why: A leader is a person who guides a group and helps it, like a teacher.

check.q: Who leads the whole school?
check.why: Mr. Green is the principal. He leads the whole school and makes rules for every class.

check.q: What does the crossing guard do?
choices: Stops cars so kids can cross
check.why: Ms. Lee holds up her sign. The cars stop. Then kids can cross safely.

review.q: Why is there a rule about running in the hall?
choices: Someone could fall and get hurt
review.why: Sam ran and fell. The rule keeps kids safe.

review.q: Five kids share one swing by counting to twenty. What does that rule do?
review.why: Everyone gets a turn. That is fair.

review.q: Who makes the rules at the pool?
review.why: The lifeguard makes the rules at the pool.

review.q: How did Room Twelve pick its three rules?
review.why: Each kid put dots by the rules they liked. The top three won.

review.q: Leo grabbed a crayon. What did he do to make it right?
choices: He gave it back and said sorry
review.why: Leo gave the crayon back and said sorry. That fixed what he did.

review.q: Which person is the leader of the whole school?
review.why: The principal leads the whole school.
